2.text: of birch-wood; but the Arctic Chukchee use also various kinds of driftwood,

3.text: especially American pine, and even oak picked out from wreckage. On some

4.text: parts of the Arctic shore driftwood is piled up in large masses (Plate VII, Fig. 2),

5.text: sometimes covering an entire acre, and wreckage may be found everywhere

6.text: among the wood. The Pacific people buy lumber from whalers, or even bring

7.text: it themselves from St. Lawrence Island or the Alaskan shore in their boats.

8.text: Birch runners are fit only for the cold season, and after the end of March

9.text: will not run easily in the daytime, when the snow is damp and loose and all

10.text: the sharp points of the ground protrude. The friction of birch-wood is so

11.text: strong as to tire out the best dogs, and, besides, wear out the precious run-

12.text: ners in a couple of weeks. In the Kolyma district and in the eastern Arctic

13.text: villages, runners made from the outer layer of the larch, with twisted fibre

14.text: (called in local Russian крень), are substituted for use in springtime. The
14.note: крень, compression wood — the dense twisted-grain wood formed on the lower side of a conifer leaning on a slope. Bogoras glosses it on this line: outer layer of the larch, twisted fibre, trees on mountain-slopes, harder than ordinary larchwood. Feminine soft-stem, so pre-reform takes ь and never ъ; кренъ would be крен, a Dutch nautical loan meaning list or heel, which is not a wood. Adjudicated to кренъ as an abraded hard sign, reverted on the gloss.

15.text: material is obtained from the trees that grow on the mountain-slopes, and is

16.text: much harder than the ordinary larchwood. In the damp weather of spring

17.text: the drivers will sometimes smear the birch runners with oil, though it may spoil

18.text: them for the winter; or they will tie a piece of blubber to the quirt, and

19.text: every now and then, while going ahead, whip it across the track, to be passed

20.text: over alternately by both runners, to make them more slippery. Much more

21.text: frequently the runners are shod with whalebone, or with pieces of bone taken

22.text: from the whale’s jaw, sewed to the runner with sunken stitches (see Fig. 17, g)

23.text: or fastened with wooden pegs. On the Chukchee Peninsula, drivers protect

24.text: their wooden runners with bone shoeing throughout the winter, though it makes

25.text: the sledge twice as heavy, and the bone does not run smoothly on the cold,

27.text: In the winter-time the birch runners are covered with a thin sheet of ice

28.text: to make them run more smoothly. For this purpose they are well saturated

29.text: with water in the early fall, usually by immersing them in a pool or small

30.text: lake for a couple of weeks; or in winter, when the pools are frozen, by steaming

31.text: them in long troughs filled with hot water or by frequently wetting the bottoms

32.text: with boiling water. Only damp wood, well soaked with water, will hold

33.text: the ice-sheet, which is formed by wetting the bottoms of the runners several

34.text: times over by means of a small piece of skin. The colder the day, the hotter

35.text: the water that is used for the process. Larch-wood holds the ice-sheet only

36.text: for a short time, and bone hardly at all: therefore it is not subjected to the

37.text: process. This method of covering the runners with ice is adopted by all the

38.text: West Bering tribes. The people in South Kamchatka, however, on account

39.text: of their damp winters with frequent thaws, do not employ it much. The

40.text: Kolyma Yakut cover the runners of their reindeer and horse sledges also
